title: How to install an extension in Chrome on Mac: steps, pinning and fixes

intro: In Chrome on Mac, open the Chrome Web Store, find the extension, select Add to Chrome, then select Add extension if asked. On a Mac, Chrome installs extensions from the Chrome Web Store, and Google gives the same steps for Windows and Linux.
tldr: Open the Chrome Web Store in Chrome on your Mac, then select Add to Chrome on the extension's page.
If Chrome asks, select Add extension. Chrome on Mac installs from the store, not from downloaded files.
Pin the extension from the Extensions icon next to the address bar, which looks like a puzzle piece.
Manage installed extensions at More > Extensions > Manage extensions, or type chrome://extensions in the address bar.

blocks.text: Before you install: what you need

You need Google Chrome on your Mac and a regular browsing window. If you don't have Chrome yet, you can download it from Google's Chrome page at google.com/chrome. Open Chrome before you start, then check the window you are using. Chrome doesn't allow extension installs in Incognito mode or as a guest, so the install fails there before it begins. A normal window works. Keep the store page open in that same window, so you don't mix up tabs.
Why Chrome on Mac installs extensions only from the store

Google's developer documentation says installs on Windows and macOS must come from the Chrome Web Store. Double-clicking a downloaded extension file won't install it. Since Chrome 44, Chrome on Mac doesn't allow external installs from a path to a local CRX file. The rule keeps one checkpoint between you and the extension. It also means you have one install route to learn, not several. Google's help pages give the same steps for Mac, Windows, and Linux.
Read the listing before you select Add to Chrome

A store listing gives you clues, and they are quick to check. Look at the publisher name, the written description, and the number of users shown. Scale matters here. Exstats counted 221,717 published Chrome Web Store extensions as of June 30, 2026. The median Chrome extension has 14 users, according to the same report. Chrome user counts are cumulative, so they don't compare directly with Firefox or Edge numbers. A clear publisher and a specific description are better signs than a flashy name.
Why searches can lead you to a bad extension

Searching for an extension can lead to a bad one, even inside the official store. Socket researcher John Tuckner identified 319 Chrome extensions with an estimated 13.4 million installs over a decade that hijacked searches. The extensions were in the Chrome Web Store, and most were unlisted. Malwarebytes reported the findings in an article dated October 30, 2026. The practical lesson is simple. Install the extension you searched for by name, from a listing you opened yourself.
Read the install prompt before you confirm

When you select Add to Chrome, Chrome shows a prompt that lists what the extension can access. Read it before you continue. An extension that can read and change data on every site you visit has wide reach. Some tools really need that, such as a password manager or a page translator. A note-taking extension that asks for access to every site is a question to answer first. If Enhanced protection is on, Chrome can also flag an extension as not trusted. Chrome's help page describes that warning as a choice between Continue to install and Close.
A worked example from start to finish

Say you want a tool that saves web pages as PDF files. Open a new tab with ⌘T, then search the Chrome Web Store for the name you saw in an article. Pick the result from the publisher you expected. Read the description, then select Add to Chrome. Read the prompt, and select Add extension if Chrome asks. When the install finishes, open the Extensions menu, find the tool, and pin it. Each step happens in the same window, so you can always see where you are.
Pin and manage extensions in Chrome on Mac

Installed extensions go into the Extensions menu next to the address bar. That menu icon looks like a puzzle piece. A pinned extension gets its own icon in the toolbar, so one click opens it. Pin the ones you use every day and leave the rest in the menu. Right-click, or Control-click, a pinned icon and choose Unpin to hide it again. Some extensions don't offer pinning, and that is normal.

The management page lists every extension you installed. From there you can turn an extension on or off without removing it. Select Details to change whether it runs in Incognito, and to set its site access. Site access has three choices: On select, On specific sites, and On all sites. To remove an extension, right-click its icon and choose Remove from Chrome. Turning an extension off first is a good test if it seems to cause trouble.
Fix Chrome extension install errors on Mac

Most install errors fall into a few groups. Chrome blocks installs in Incognito and guest sessions. It disables some extensions that no longer meet requirements. It also marks some extensions as corrupted. Each group has its own fix, so start by reading the exact message. The messages in the troubleshooting list come from Google's help pages, so you can match them word for word.

Corrupted extensions need a different fix. Open the management page, then select Repair, then Repair extension. If the extension is still corrupted after the repair, run anti-malware software on your Mac, then repair it again. Keep that order. Repairing first tells you whether the problem is the extension or something else on the Mac.
Where extensions won't install at all

Some places block installs by design. Chrome doesn't allow extension installs in Incognito mode or as a guest. Work or school computers can block some extensions, because an administrator sets that policy. On a managed Mac, you may hit a block you can't lift yourself. Ask your IT team which extensions are allowed. Don't try to get around a block on a work machine, even if the extension looks harmless.
Mistakes people make when installing on a Mac

The most common mistake is hunting for a .crx file to double-click. Since Chrome 44, Chrome on Mac won't install an extension that way from a local file. Another mistake is downloading from a site that isn't the store. Those files skip the store listing, so you lose the publisher details. A third mistake is installing an extension and forgetting it. Review the list every few months, and remove what you no longer use.
Keyboard shortcuts for the install steps

Shortcuts speed up the install route without changing the steps. Press ⌘T to open a new tab for the store. Press ⌘L to jump to the address bar, then type chrome://extensions to reach the management page. Press ⌘, to open Settings. Google's shortcut page lists no key for Extensions or the Chrome Web Store, so the menu path is the one to learn.
Some navigation options on a Mac need Full Keyboard Access turned on in System Settings. If a key doesn't respond the way Google's list says, check that setting first.
What to check after the install

Test the extension on one page before you rely on it. Check that it does what its listing says, and that it doesn't change pages you didn't expect. Look at its site access again if a page behaves oddly. Then decide whether it stays pinned. A short list of extensions is easier to audit than a long one.
Related Chrome guides on this site

If an install won't start in your current window, try a normal window first. The guide on [how to open an incognito window in Chrome on Mac](/how-to/open-an-incognito-window-in-chrome) explains the two ways to get there. If you keep extensions for work and home separately, [how to create a Chrome profile on Mac](/how-to/create-a-chrome-profile-in-chrome) shows how to split them.

faq.question: Can I install a Chrome extension on a Mac from a downloaded file?
faq.answer: Usually no. Chrome's developer documentation says installs on macOS must come from the Chrome Web Store. Since Chrome 44, Chrome on Mac doesn't allow external installs from a path to a local CRX file. If an extension isn't in the store, check the developer's official website before you look elsewhere.

faq.question: Why don't I see an Add to Chrome button on the extension page?
faq.answer: Check that you are in a regular window, not Incognito or a guest session, because installs don't work in either. If you're on a work Mac, your admin may block the extension. If the steps above don't help, ask the extension's publisher or your IT team.

faq.question: Can I use an extension in Incognito?
faq.answer: Yes, if you allow it. Open the management page, select Details, and turn on Allow in incognito. Chrome still won't install a new extension while you're in an Incognito window.

faq.question: How do I remove an extension from Chrome on a Mac?
faq.answer: Right-click the extension's icon in the toolbar or the Extensions menu, then choose Remove from Chrome. If you want to keep it for later, turn it off on the management page instead.

faq.question: What is the difference between turning off and removing an extension?
faq.answer: Turning off keeps the extension installed but inactive, so you can switch it on later. Removing deletes it from Chrome. If an extension acts strangely, turn it off first to test, then remove it if the problem goes away.

faq.question: Why does Chrome say an extension is not trusted by Enhanced Safe Browsing?
faq.answer: That message appears when Enhanced protection is on and Chrome doesn't trust the extension. Choose Close if you don't know where it came from. Choose Continue to install only if you trust the source and need the extension.

faq.question: How can I tell if a Chrome extension is safe?
faq.answer: No single signal proves it. Check the publisher, read the description, review the permissions, and be wary of search results you didn't ask for. Reports show that some extensions in the store hijacked searches, so check your list after each install.

task: Install a Chrome extension on a Mac
appliesTo: Google Chrome on macOS, installing from the Chrome Web Store
requirements: Google Chrome installed on your Mac
A regular browsing window, not Incognito or a guest session
Permission to install extensions, if your work or school Mac is managed
The extension's name or a store page you trust

steps.name: Open the Chrome Web Store
steps.text: Open Google Chrome on your Mac. Press ⌘T for a new tab, then go to the Chrome Web Store. If you don't have it bookmarked, search for Chrome Web Store in Google and open the official result.
steps.tip: Check the page title says Chrome Web Store before you search for anything.

steps.name: Find the extension and open its page
steps.text: Use the search box at the top of the store. Type the extension's name, then pick the result from its publisher. Open the listing and read the description before you continue.
steps.tip: Ads and lookalike results can look official. Compare the name with the store listing.

steps.name: Select Add to Chrome
steps.text: On the extension's page, select Add to Chrome. Chrome opens a prompt that lists what the extension can access. Read that list before you confirm anything.
steps.tip: If the list asks for more access than the job needs, close the prompt and look for another extension.

steps.name: Confirm with Add extension
steps.text: If Chrome asks you to confirm, select Add extension. A trusted extension shows this option. If you see a warning about Enhanced Safe Browsing, read the troubleshooting section before you choose anything.
steps.tip: Choose Close if you are unsure. You can install it again later.

steps.name: Wait for the install to finish
steps.text: Chrome installs the extension and adds it to the Extensions menu next to the address bar. Some extensions open a setup or welcome page. Follow its steps, or close the page if you don't need it.

steps.name: Pin the extension to the toolbar
steps.text: Select the Extensions icon next to the address bar. It looks like a puzzle piece. Find your extension in the list and select Pin. Pinned extensions stay visible in the toolbar.
steps.tip: Some extensions don't offer pinning. They stay in the Extensions menu.

steps.name: Open the extensions management page
steps.text: To see everything you installed, select More (the three dots at the top right), then Extensions, then Manage extensions. You can also type chrome://extensions in the address bar. Both routes open the same page.

steps.name: Check the switch and site access
steps.text: On the management page, make sure the extension's switch is on. Select Details to see its site access. Choose On select, On specific sites, or On all sites. Pick the narrowest setting that still works.
steps.tip: Changing site access is a setting, not an uninstall. You can change it again any time.

troubleshooting.problem: Installs fail or the button does nothing in a window
troubleshooting.fix: Chrome doesn't allow extension installs in Incognito mode or as a guest. Open a regular window, then install again from the store page.

troubleshooting.problem: Dialog says This extension is not trusted by Enhanced Safe Browsing
troubleshooting.fix: Enhanced protection flags extensions Chrome doesn't trust. Choose Close if you don't know the source. Choose Continue to install only if you trust the publisher and need the extension.

troubleshooting.problem: Extension is disabled and won't turn on
troubleshooting.fix: Chrome may disable extensions that no longer meet requirements. Try re-enabling it on the management page, but only within the limited time Chrome allows. On a work or school Mac, an administrator has to re-enable it.
Open the management page, select Repair, then Repair extension. If it's still corrupted, run anti-malware software on your Mac, then repair it again.

troubleshooting.problem: Install is blocked on a work or school Mac
troubleshooting.fix: Work or school computers may block some extensions. Ask your IT team which extensions are allowed. Don't try to bypass the block.

troubleshooting.problem: I downloaded a .crx file and double-clicked it
troubleshooting.fix: Since Chrome 44, Chrome on Mac doesn't allow installs from a local CRX file. Delete the file and install the extension from the Chrome Web Store instead.
